title: U.S. Government Takes 10% Stake in Intel

sentences.text: President Donald Trump announced that the federal government will receive a 10% stake in Intel.
sentences.evidence: On Aug. 22, President Donald Trump announced that the federal government had obtained a 10% stake in Intel, the computer chip designer and fabricator.

sentences.text: The government will acquire 433.3 million shares at $20.47 per share.
sentences.evidence: The company's press release said the government purchased 433.3 million primary shares of the stock at $20.47 per share, equaling 9.9%.

sentences.text: The transaction is valued at about $8.9 billion.
sentences.evidence: Chipmaker Intel has agreed to give the U.S. government a nearly 10% stake in its business... the U.S. government will buy $8.9 billion in Intel common stock.

sentences.text: Nearly $6 billion of the purchase will be funded with previously awarded CHIPS Act grants that have not yet been paid.
sentences.evidence: Nearly $6 billion of that will be funded with previously awarded, but not yet paid, grants from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act.

sentences.text: For builders, the key point is that the government is using existing grant commitments rather than new cash.
Intel will not grant the government any voting or board seats.
sentences.evidence: Intel said the government’s investment will not include voting or governance power.

sentences.text: A warrant gives the White House an option to buy an additional 5% of shares within five years if Intel’s foundry business falls below 51% ownership.
sentences.evidence: The agreement includes a warrant that gives the White House the option to buy another 5% of Intel’s common shares in the next five years.

sentences.text: Intel received $8.5 billion in grants and $11 billion in loans from the Biden administration for new U.S. fabs.
sentences.evidence: Last year, Biden awarded Intel $8.5 billion in grants and $11 billion in loans, plus tax credits, with the expectation that the company would build plants in Arizona, New Mexico, Ohio and Oregon.

sentences.text: The CHIPS and Science Act, signed in 2022, set aside $53 billion for semiconductor incentives.
sentences.evidence: In 2022, President Joe Biden signed the CHIPS and Science Act into law, which ... set aside $53 billion in incentives for manufacturing, research and development.

sentences.text: The stake therefore links the financing program directly to an equity position, a departure from typical grant-only models.
Intel’s market capitalization is just over $100 billion.
sentences.evidence: The struggling Silicon Valley chipmaker has a market cap of just over $100 billion.

sentences.text: Intel reported a loss of nearly $19 billion last year after a $1.7 billion profit in 2023.
sentences.evidence: The company reported a loss of nearly $19 billion last year, after recording a $1.7 billion profit in 2023.

sentences.text: Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley criticized the deal as harmful to the semiconductor sector.
sentences.evidence: Sen. Ron Wyden ... said it is "nothing more than corporate extortion..." and Sen. Jeff Merkley said the move would hurt the semiconductor industry.

sentences.text: Republican senators Thom Tillis and Rand Paul opposed the stake, while Senator Bernie Sanders expressed support.
sentences.evidence: Many in Trump's own party, such as Sen. Thom Tillis, R‑N.C., and Sen. Rand Paul, R‑Ky., have opposed the move, while some left‑leaning lawmakers like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I‑Vt., have said they support it.

sentences.text: The split highlights how the deal sits at the intersection of national‑security priorities and concerns about government overreach.
For technology builders, the government's equity stake signals a new model of public‑private partnership that could shape future financing of critical chip capacity.
If the warrant is exercised, the government's ownership could rise to roughly 15%, potentially influencing strategic decisions without formal voting rights.
The arrangement also raises questions about precedent: will other strategic industries see similar equity injections, or will backlash curb such moves?
Ultimately, the stake ties taxpayer‑funded incentives directly to corporate performance, creating both accountability and a new risk profile for public money.
